claim: Complexins play activating and inhibitory functions in neurotransmitter release.
source: Complexins play activating and inhibitory functions in neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is a general statement about complexin function that is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript and citations to prior work.

claim: The complexin accessory helix inhibits release.
source: The complexin accessory helix inhibits release and was proposed to insert into SNARE complexes to prevent their full assembly.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in the manuscript and references to prior work.

claim: The complexin accessory helix was proposed to insert into SNARE complexes to prevent their full assembly.
source: The complexin accessory helix inhibits release and was proposed to insert into SNARE complexes to prevent their full assembly.
evidence: This refers to a model proposed in prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The insertion model was supported by 'superclamp' and 'poor-clamp' mutations that enhanced or decreased the complexin-I inhibitory activity in cell–cell fusion assays.
source: This model was supported by 'superclamp' and 'poor-clamp' mutations that enhanced or decreased the complexin-I inhibitory activity in cell–cell fusion assays, and by the crystal structure of a superclamp mutant bound to a synaptobrevin-truncated SNARE complex.
evidence: This refers to prior experimental evidence from cell-cell fusion assays.

claim: The insertion model was supported by the crystal structure of a superclamp mutant bound to a synaptobrevin-truncated SNARE complex.
source: This model was supported by 'superclamp' and 'poor-clamp' mutations that enhanced or decreased the complexin-I inhibitory activity in cell–cell fusion assays, and by the crystal structure of a superclamp mutant bound to a synaptobrevin-truncated SNARE complex.
evidence: This refers to prior structural evidence from crystallography.

claim: NMR studies show that the complexin-I accessory helix does not insert into synaptobrevin-truncated SNARE complexes in solution.
source: NMR studies now show that the complexin-I accessory helix does not insert into synaptobrevin-truncated SNARE complexes in solution
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by NMR data presented in Figures 2-6.

claim: Superclamp mutants have slightly stimulatory or no effects on neurotransmitter release.
source: electrophysiological data reveal that superclamp mutants have slightly stimulatory or no effects on neurotransmitter release
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 7.

claim: A poor-clamp mutant inhibits neurotransmitter release.
source: whereas a poor-clamp mutant inhibits release
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 7.

claim: Increasing the negative charge of the complexin-I accessory helix inhibits neurotransmitter release.
source: Importantly, increasing or decreasing the negative charge of the complexin-I accessory helix inhibits or stimulates release, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9.

claim: Decreasing the negative charge of the complexin-I accessory helix stimulates neurotransmitter release.
source: Importantly, increasing or decreasing the negative charge of the complexin-I accessory helix inhibits or stimulates release, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9.

claim: The complexin accessory helix inhibits release through electrostatic and perhaps steric repulsion enabled by its location between the vesicle and plasma membranes.
source: These results suggest a new model whereby the complexin accessory helix inhibits release through electrostatic (and perhaps steric) repulsion enabled by its location between the vesicle and plasma membranes.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data and structural considerations.

claim: Neurotransmitter release is crucial for interneuronal communication.
source: Neurotransmitter release is crucial for interneuronal communication and is exquisitely regulated by a sophisticated protein machinery (Sudhof, 2013).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Basic aspects of neurotransmitter release have been reconstituted with eight central components of the release machinery.
source: basic aspects of this process have been reconstituted with eight central components of the release machinery (Ma et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The neuronal SNAREs synaptobrevin, syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25 form a tight four-helix bundle called the SNARE complex.
source: the neuronal soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptors (SNAREs) synaptobrevin, syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25 form a tight four-helix bundle called the SNARE complex (Sollner et al., 1993; Poirier et al., 1998; Sutton et al., 1998)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The SNARE complex brings the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes together.
source: that brings the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes together (Hanson et al., 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The SNARE complex is critical for membrane fusion.
source: that brings the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes together (Hanson et al., 1997) and is critical for membrane fusion
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the context and citations.

claim: NSF and SNAPs disassemble the SNARE complex.
source: N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor (NSF) and soluble NSF attachment proteins (SNAPs) disassemble the SNARE complex (Sollner et al., 1993)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: NSF and SNAPs recycle the SNAREs for another round of fusion.
source: to recycle the SNAREs for another round of fusion (Mayer et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: NSF and SNAPs may favor physiological membrane fusion by disassembling syntaxin-1-SNAP-25 complexes.
source: and may favor physiological membrane fusion by disassembling syntaxin-1-SNAP-25 complexes (Ma et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Munc18-1 and Munc13s orchestrate SNARE complex assembly in an NSF/SNAP resistant manner.
source: Munc18-1 and Munc13s orchestrate SNARE complex assembly in an NSF/SNAP resistant manner (Ma et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Munc18-1 and Munc13s may play a direct role in fusion.
source: and may play a direct role in fusion (Dulubova et al., 2007; Li et al., 2011b)
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Synaptotagmin-1 acts as a Ca2+ sensor.
source: and synaptotagmin-1 acts as a Ca2+ sensor (Fernandez-Chacon et al., 2001)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Synaptotagmin-1 likely bridges the two membranes.
source: likely by bridging the two membranes (Arac et al., 2006; Xue et al., 2008a)
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Complexins are small soluble proteins that bind to the SNARE complex.
source: Tight regulation of neurotransmitter release also depends critically on complexins, small soluble proteins that bind to the SNARE complex (McMahon et al., 1995)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Absence of complexins leads to a severe impairment of Ca2+-evoked exocytosis.
source: Absence of complexins leads to a severe impairment of Ca2+-evoked exocytosis and to varied effects on spontaneous release ranging from small decreases to dramatic increases, depending on the system (Reim et al., 2001; Huntwork and Littleton, 2007; Xue et al., 2008b; Maximov et al., 2009; Hobson et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Absence of complexins leads to varied effects on spontaneous release ranging from small decreases to dramatic increases, depending on the system.
source: Absence of complexins leads to a severe impairment of Ca2+-evoked exocytosis and to varied effects on spontaneous release ranging from small decreases to dramatic increases, depending on the system (Reim et al., 2001; Huntwork and Littleton, 2007; Xue et al., 2008b; Maximov et al., 2009; Hobson et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The effects of complexin absence likely arise from an interplay between stimulatory and inhibitory activities of different regions of complexins.
source: These results likely arise from an interplay between stimulatory and inhibitory activities of different regions of complexins (Xue et al., 2007, 2009; Cho et al., 2010; Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Complexin I is largely unstructured in solution.
source: Complexin I (CpxI) is largely unstructured in solution (Pabst et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Complexin I forms a central α-helix that binds to the SNARE complex and is preceded by an accessory helix.
source: but forms a central α-helix that binds to the SNARE complex and is preceded by an accessory helix (Bracher et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2002) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural work and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The central helix of complexin is crucial for both the activating and inhibitory functions of complexins.
source: The central helix is crucial for both the activating and inhibitory functions of complexins, while the accessory helix inhibits release (Xue et al., 2007; Maximov et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The complexin N-terminus plays an activating function, releasing the inhibition by the accessory helix.
source: the complexin N-terminus plays an activating function, releasing the inhibition by the accessory helix (Xue et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The complexin C-terminal sequence has activating and inhibitory roles.
source: and the C-terminal sequence has activating and inhibitory roles (Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The crystal structure of the CpxI(26-83)/SNARE complex shows the accessory helix does not contact the SNARE complex.
source: Cross-peaks from the accessory helix, which does not contact the SNARE complex, are also perturbed by binding because the stabilization of the central helix propagates toward the accessory helix
evidence: This is inferred from the crystal structure and NMR data discussed in the text.

claim: The 1H-15N TROSY-HSQC spectrum of CpxI(26-83) exhibits sharp cross-peaks and poor dispersion because the fragment is very flexible.
source: As described previously (Chen et al., 2002), the 1H-15N TROSY-HSQC spectrum of this fragment exhibits sharp cross-peaks and poor dispersion (Figure 2A) because, although partially helical, the fragment is very flexible.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Upon binding to SNARE complex, the 1H-15N TROSY-HSQC spectrum of CpxI(26-83) reveals strong broadening and a dramatic increase in dispersion for cross-peaks from the central helix.
source: Upon binding to a minimal SNARE complex containing the SNAREs motifs of synaptobrevin, syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25 (below referred to as SNARE complex or SC), the 1H-15N TROSY-HSQC spectrum of CpxI(26-83) reveals strong broadening and a dramatic increase in dispersion for cross-peaks from the central helix (Figure 2B, red contours)
evidence: This is a direct observation from NMR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The strong broadening and dramatic increase in dispersion for cross-peaks from the central helix is due to stable packing of this helix against the synaptobrevin and syntaxin-1 SNARE motifs.
source: due to stable packing of this helix against the synaptobrevin and syntaxin-1 SNARE motifs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the NMR data based on structural knowledge.

claim: The synaptobrevin C-terminal truncations increase the flexibility of the accessory helix.
source: These data show that the synaptobrevin C-terminal truncations increase the flexibility of the accessory helix, in correlation with the destabilization of N-terminal part of the central helix
evidence: This is an interpretation of the NMR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The NMR data provide very strong evidence against the notion that the accessory helix of CpxI(26-83) inserts into the groove generated by synaptobrevin truncations.
source: and provide very strong evidence against the notion that the accessory helix of CpxI(26-83) inserts into the grove generated by the truncations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NMR data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The accessory helix does not insert into the groove left by the Δ60 truncation.
source: The well-resolved cross-peaks from the accessory helix of CpxI(26-83) bound to SCΔ60 (e.g., those of A30 and Q38) had similar intensities as those observed upon binding to SCΔ62, showing that the accessory helix does not insert into the groove left by the Δ60 truncation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from NMR data comparing different truncations.

claim: WT CpxI(26-48) does not bind to the synaptobrevin Δ60 truncated SNARE complex in solution.
source: Hence, these results clearly show that CpxI(26-48) does not bind to the synaptobrevin Δ60 truncated SNARE complex in solution under the conditions of our experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from NMR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The accessory helix of CpxI(26-83) superclamp mutant does not bind to SCΔ60 under the conditions of the NMR experiments.
source: Therefore, we were unable to detect an interaction between the accessory helix of CpxI(26-83)supcl and SCΔ60 under the conditions of our NMR experiments
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There may be a weak interaction between the accessory helix of CpxI(26-83) superclamp mutant and SCΔ60 in solution that becomes stabilized by crystallization.
source: although we cannot rule out the possibility that there is a weak interaction in solution that becomes stabilized by crystallization.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible explanation for the discrepancy between NMR and crystallography data.

claim: The synaptobrevin truncations lead to flexibility in the C-terminal half of the SNAP-25 C-terminal SNARE motif.
source: These results show that the synaptobrevin truncations lead to flexibility in the C-terminal half of SNC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from NMR data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: For the Δ62 truncation, stable structure in the SNAP-25 C-terminal SNARE motif appears to remain only up to residue 180.
source: For the Δ62 truncation, stable structure appears to remain only up to residue 180.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from NMR data.

claim: CpxI(26-83) binding induced practically no changes in the cross-peaks corresponding to the flexible C-terminus of SNC in the Δ62 SNARE complex.
source: Importantly, CpxI(26-83) binding induced practically no changes in the cross-peaks corresponding to the flexible C-terminus of SNC in the Δ62 SNARE complex (Figure 3C), showing again that the CpxI accessory helix does not interact with the truncated SNARE complex.
evidence: This is a direct observation from NMR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Addition of CpxI(26-48) caused practically no changes on the 1H-15N HSQC spectrum of 2H,15N-SNC-SCΔ62.
source: Finally, addition of a CpxI fragment spanning only the accessory helix [CpxI(26-48)] caused practically no changes on the 1H-15N HSQC spectrum of 2H,15N-SNC-SCΔ62 (Figure 3D), confirming that the accessory helix does not bind by itself to the truncated SNARE complex or binds with extremely weak affinity.
evidence: This is a direct observation from NMR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The Δ62 synaptobrevin truncation led to flexibility in the C-terminal half of the syntaxin-1 SNARE motif.
source: These results correlated with those obtained with 2H,15N-SNC-SCΔ62 and indicate that the C-terminal half of the syntaxin-1 SNARE motif becomes flexible due to the Δ62 synaptobrevin truncation
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from NMR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CpxI(26-83) binding did not yield new well-dispersed cross-peaks that might correspond to structured syntaxin-1 C-terminal residues interacting with the CpxI(26-83) accessory helix.
source: Although these data are less conclusive than those obtained with the 2H,15N-SNC-SCΔ62 complex, it is clear that CpxI(26-83) binding did not yield new well-dispersed cross-peaks that might correspond to structured syntaxin-1 C-terminal residues interacting with the CpxI(26-83) accessory helix.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from NMR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The affinity of CpxI(47-134) for the non-truncated SNARE complex is Kd = 339 ± 9 nM.
source: For the latter (Figure 4A), we measured a Kd of 339 ± 9 nM (ΔH = −32.6 kcal/mol; N = 0.95)
evidence: This is a direct measurement from ITC data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The affinity of CpxI(47-134) for SCΔ60 is Kd = 2.39 ± 0.19 μM.
source: Importantly, binding of Cpx(47-134) to SCΔ60 was even weaker, with a Kd of 2.39 ± 0.19 μM (ΔH = −19.5 kcal/mol; N = 0.92) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from ITC data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Binding of CpxI(47-134) to SCΔ60 is not saturated upon addition of 1.5 equivalents of CpxI(47-134).
source: This decreased affinity implies that binding of CpxI(47-134) to SCΔ60 is not saturated upon addition of 1.5 equivalents of CpxI(47-134) (arrow in Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ITC data and the measured Kd value.

claim: The heat observed upon addition of CpxI(26-83) to SCΔ60 blocked with CpxI(27-134) arises from completion of the titration of the central helix binding site, rather than from interactions involving the accessory helix.
source: Hence, the heat observed upon addition of CpxI(26-83) to SCΔ60 blocked with CpxI(27-134) arises from completion of the titration of the central helix binding site, rather than from interactions involving the accessory helix.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ITC data and analysis.

claim: No binding of the accessory helix of Cpx(26-83) to SCΔ60 is detected in ITC experiments.
source: Hence, no binding of the accessory helix of Cpx(26-83) to SCΔ60 is detected in these experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from ITC data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ITC data reproduce the results of Kummel et al. (2011) within experimental error.
source: Although the Kd is somewhat different, we consider that our data do reproduce the results of Kummel et al. (2011) within experimental error, considering the approximation involved in the single-site model.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current ITC data with prior published results.

claim: The interpretation of the competition ITC assays needs to be revised.
source: However, our results show that the interpretation of the competition ITC assays needs to be revised and that these assays are unable to detect an interaction between the accessory helix of WT CpxI(26-83) and SCΔ60, in agreement with our NMR results.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ITC data and analysis.

claim: The competition ITC assays are unable to detect an interaction between the accessory helix of WT CpxI(26-83) and SCΔ60.
source: However, our results show that the interpretation of the competition ITC assays needs to be revised and that these assays are unable to detect an interaction between the accessory helix of WT CpxI(26-83) and SCΔ60, in agreement with our NMR results.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ITC data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The accessory helix of the CpxI(26-83) superclamp mutant does not interact with SNARE complexes containing C-terminally truncated synaptobrevin in solution.
source: These results contrast with those described previously (Kummel et al., 2011) but agree with our NMR data and further suggest that even the accessory helix of the CpxI(26-83)supcl mutant does not interact with SNARE complexes containing C-terminally truncated synaptobrevin in solution or, if there is any interaction, it is weak and cannot be detected in our NMR and ITC experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from ITC data shown in Figure 4E and NMR data.

claim: The C-terminal half of the synaptobrevin SNARE motif is flexible in 2H,15N-Syb-SCΔ236 as a result of the syntaxin-1 truncation.
source: These results suggest that the C-terminal half of the synaptobrevin SNARE motif is flexible in 2H,15N-Syb-SCΔ236 as a result of the syntaxin-1 truncation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from NMR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The C-terminus of SNAP-25 C-terminal SNARE motif becomes flexible upon truncation of syntaxin-1.
source: These changes are similar to those caused by the synaptobrevin truncation in 2H,15N-SNC-SCΔ62 (Figure 3B) and show that the C-terminus of SNC also becomes flexible upon truncation of syntaxin-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from NMR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The accessory helix of CpxI(26-83) does not interact with the SNAP-25 C-terminus in the syntaxin-1 truncated SNARE complex.
source: While the results obtained with 2H,15N-SNC-SCΔ236 show that the accessory helix of CpxI(26-83) does not interact with the SNAP-25 C-terminus in the syntaxin-1 truncated SNARE complex and hence does not insert into the complex
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from NMR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The accessory helix does not interact with the synaptobrevin SNARE motif of the syntaxin-1 truncated SNARE complexes.
source: Regardless of the validity of this explanation, it is clear from the behavior of the cross-peaks of the accessory helix that this helix does not interact with the synaptobrevin SNARE motif of the syntaxin-1 truncated SNARE complexes, arguing against the model of Figure 1D.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from NMR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The D27L, E34F, R37A superclamp mutation did not change the ability to rescue the complexin I-III KO phenotype.
source: The D27L, E34F, R37A superclamp mutation that introduces hydrophobic residues in the CpxI accessory helix did not change the ability to rescue the complexin I-III KO phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The amplitudes of action potential-evoked EPSCs tended to be larger for the D27L, E34F, R37A superclamp mutant than those observed upon rescue with WT CpxI.
source: On the contrary the amplitudes of action potential-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) tended to be larger that those observed upon rescue with WT CpxI (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The calculated Pvr was slightly increased in the rescue with the superclamp CpxI mutants.
source: As the size of the readily releasable pool (RRP) measured by hypertonic solution (Rosenmund and Stevens, 1996) was unchanged, the calculated Pvr was also slightly increased in the rescue with the superclamp CpxI mutants (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: The K26A mutation impaired full rescue of the KO phenotype.
source: Conversely, the 'non-clamping' K26A mutation impaired full rescue of the KO phenotype, as the EPSC amplitude and Pvr were reduced, and the PPR was increased (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7B-E.

claim: The effects of superclamp and poor-clamp CpxI mutations on neurotransmitter release do not correlate with their effects on cell–cell fusion assays.
source: Overall, these results are in contrast with key predictions from the insertion and zigzag models and do not correlate with the data obtained with cell–cell fusion assays (Giraudo et al., 2009)
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by comparing the electrophysiological data with prior cell-cell fusion data.

claim: The functional data did not support the hypothesis that the inhibitory activity of the accessory helix arises from insertion into the SNARE complex to replace part of the synaptobrevin SNARE motif.
source: Hence, our functional data did not support the hypothesis that the inhibitory activity of the accessory helix arises from insertion into the SNARE complex to replace part of the synaptobrevin SNARE motif, in correlation with our NMR and ITC results.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data in Figure 7.

claim: A dramatic increase in spontaneous release is observed in the absence of Drosophila complexin.
source: In search of an alternative model that could explain the inhibitory function of the complexin accessory helix, we turned our attention to complexin from Drosophila melanogaster (dmCpx) because a dramatic increase in spontaneous release is observed in its absence (Huntwork and Littleton, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Experiments with chimeras of murine CpxI and dmCpx suggested that the accessory helix of dmCpx inhibits release more strongly than that of murine CpxI in mouse hippocampal neurons.
source: and experiments with chimeras of murine CpxI and dmCpx suggested that the accessory helix of dmCpx inhibits release more strongly than that of murine CpxI in mouse hippocampal neurons (Xue et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: No significant differences in evoked EPSC amplitudes, RRP charge and Pvr were observed between neurons expressing the dmAcc-CpxI chimera or WT CpxI.
source: No significant differences in evoked EPSC amplitudes, RRP charge and Pvr were observed between neurons expressing the dmAcc-CpxI chimera or WT CpxI (Figure 8B–D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8B-D.

claim: A ca. 30% reduction in the frequency of spontaneous release was observed in KO neurons expressing dmAcc-CpxI compared to KO neurons expressing WT CpxI.
source: Interestingly however, we did observe a significant, ca. 30% reduction in the frequency of spontaneous release in KO neurons expressing dmAcc-CpxI compared to KO neurons expressing WT CpxI, while the amplitudes of the miniature EPSCs (mEPSCs) were not different (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The accessory alpha helix of dmCpx contains some feature(s) that renders it more inhibitory than the accessory helix of mammalian CpxI.
source: These results indicate that the accessory alpha helix of dmCpx contains some feature(s) that renders it more inhibitory than the accessory helix of mammalian CpxI.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The accessory helix of dmCpx contains only one hydrophobic residue, like mammalian CpxI.
source: The accessory helix of dmCpx contains only one hydrophobic residue, like mammalian CpxI (Figure 8A)
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequence comparison shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Hydrophobicity does not explain the enhanced inhibitory activity of the dmCpx accessory helix.
source: therefore, hydrophobicity does not explain the enhanced inhibitory activity of the dmCpx accessory helix.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from sequence comparison and functional data.

claim: The accessory helix of dmCpx is longer and more negatively charged than that of mammalian CpxI.
source: Sequence comparisons suggest that the accessory helix of dmCpx is longer and more negatively charged than that of mammalian CpxI.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from sequence comparison.

claim: Rescue with the negatively charged CpxI-5E mutant yielded slightly reduced EPSC amplitudes.
source: Lenti-viral expression of the positively charged CpxI-3R and WT CpxI in complexin I-III triple KO neurons did not reveal significant differences in EPSC amplitudes, but rescue with the negatively charged CpxI-5E mutant yielded slightly reduced EPSC amplitudes (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The Pvr in the CpxI-3R mutant showed a tendency towards higher release probability.
source: Calculation of the Pvr showed similar release probabilities, with a tendency in the CpxI-3R mutant towards higher release probability, and a tendency in the CpxI-5E mutant towards lower probability (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The Pvr in the CpxI-5E mutant showed a tendency towards lower release probability.
source: Calculation of the Pvr showed similar release probabilities, with a tendency in the CpxI-3R mutant towards higher release probability, and a tendency in the CpxI-5E mutant towards lower probability (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Expressing the negatively charged CpxI-5E protein did not rescue the KO phenotype to the same extent as WT CpxI.
source: However, expressing the negatively charged CpxI-5E protein did not rescue this KO phenotype to the same extent, and the PPR in CpxI-5E expressing neurons was significantly increased compared to WT CpxI expressing neurons (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Complexin I-III KO neurons expressing the positively charged CpxI-3R exhibited a considerable increase in mEPSC frequency.
source: Importantly, complexin I-III KO neurons expressing the positively charged CpxI-3R exhibited a considerable increase in mEPSC frequency, whereas expression of the negatively charged CpxI-5E resulted in a significant decrease in mEPSC frequency compared to the WT CpxI expressing KO neurons (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: Expression of the negatively charged CpxI-5E resulted in a significant decrease in mEPSC frequency compared to the WT CpxI expressing KO neurons.
source: Importantly, complexin I-III KO neurons expressing the positively charged CpxI-3R exhibited a considerable increase in mEPSC frequency, whereas expression of the negatively charged CpxI-5E resulted in a significant decrease in mEPSC frequency compared to the WT CpxI expressing KO neurons (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: The accessory alpha helix of CpxI exerts its inhibitory function at least in part through the presence of negatively charged residues.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the accessory alpha helix of CpxI exerts its inhibitory function at least in part through the presence of negatively charged residues and that changes towards a more positively or more negatively charged nature result in decrease or increase of the inhibitory effect on spontaneous neurotransmitter release, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Changes towards a more positively charged accessory helix result in decrease of the inhibitory effect on spontaneous neurotransmitter release.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the accessory alpha helix of CpxI exerts its inhibitory function at least in part through the presence of negatively charged residues and that changes towards a more positively or more negatively charged nature result in decrease or increase of the inhibitory effect on spontaneous neurotransmitter release, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Changes towards a more negatively charged accessory helix result in increase of the inhibitory effect on spontaneous neurotransmitter release.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the accessory alpha helix of CpxI exerts its inhibitory function at least in part through the presence of negatively charged residues and that changes towards a more positively or more negatively charged nature result in decrease or increase of the inhibitory effect on spontaneous neurotransmitter release, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Absence of complexins does not alter the RRP as defined from the release induced by 500 mM hypertonic sucrose in autaptic hippocampal neurons.
source: Absence of complexins does not alter the RRP as defined from the release induced by 500 mM hypertonic sucrose in autaptic hippocampal neurons (e.g., Figures 7B, 8C and 9B)
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological data shown in Figures 7B, 8C and 9B.

claim: Absence of complexins leads to a decrease in release caused by 250 mM hypertonic sucrose.
source: but does lead to a decrease in release caused by 250 mM hypertonice sucrose (Xue et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Complexins increase the propensity of synaptic vesicles to fuse.
source: showing that complexins increase the propensity of synaptic vesicles to fuse.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the effects of complexin absence on sucrose-induced release.

claim: Expression of the less negatively charged mutant, CpxI-3R, led to clear increases in the fraction of the RRP released by 250 mM sucrose and the peak release rate.

claim: Introduction of negatively charged residues in the CpxI-5E mutant led to responses to 250 mM sucrose that resembled those of KO neurons.

claim: The charge of the accessory helix has a larger influence on the ability of synaptic vesicles to fuse in the absence of Ca2+ than upon Ca2+ influx.
source: These data exhibit some correlation with the Pvr (Figure 10C) but correlate best with the results from spontaneous release (Figures 9G, 10C), suggesting that the charge of the accessory helix has a larger influence on the ability of synaptic vesicles to fuse in the absence of Ca2+ than upon Ca2+ influx.

source: We believe that, although the arguments presented above and the overall available data argue strongly against the validity of the insertion and zigzag models, it might be premature to completely rule out these models given the complexity of this system.

claim: The electrostatic hindrance model is attractive because of its simplicity.
source: The model proposed here is attractive because of its simplicity and because it emerges naturally from the realization that the accessory helix of complexins is negatively charged (see Supplementary figure 1 of Huntwork and Littleton (2007)), together with examination of the crystal structure of the WT CpxI(26-83)/SNARE complex.
